Why Isolate, and How We Model the Transformer

Transformers provide galvanic isolation and change voltage and current levels.

In a converter that buys safety, a floating supply (high-side gate drive), large step ratios without extreme duty ratios, and multiple isolated outputs from one core.

The ideal transformer element describes the turns ratio. It neither dissipates nor stores energy.

A practical model adds magnetizing inductance and leakage inductance to represent magnetic behaviour.

The Ideal Transformer

Voltages are positive at the dots. Here \(i_1\) enters its dot and \(i_2\) leaves its dot.

\(\displaystyle v_1=\frac{N_1}{N_2}v_2\)

The element has no loss or energy storage, so \(v_1i_1=v_2i_2\). Hence

\(\displaystyle i_1=\frac{N_2}{N_1}i_2\).

Instantaneous power matches: \(p_1(t)=p_2(t)\) at every instant. Whatever waveform is applied on one side, sine wave or not, appears immediately on the other. No power is stored or delayed.

Magnetic Field and Flux

Winding currents produce the magnetic field that links both windings.

Magnetic flux density \(\mathbf B\) describes the magnetic field’s strength and direction. The component perpendicular to a surface determines how much magnetic flux passes through each unit of area.

Magnetic flux \(\Phi\) integrates that component over a surface \(A\), with chosen unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf n}\):

\(\displaystyle \Phi=\int_A\mathbf B\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA\)

For uniform, normal \(\mathbf B\): \(\Phi=BA\). Flux is measured in webers (Wb): \(1\ \mathrm{Wb}=1\ \mathrm{T\,m^2}\).

A Core Concentrates the Winding’s Flux

\(B\) is measured on the axis at winding mid-height. Flux lines are closed loops: all the flux passing up through the winding must return down through the space outside it. With air everywhere, the field spreads through the whole surrounding volume, and 100 turns at 0.10 A give only 0.47 mT.

Same turns, current and measurement point. The same current produces far more flux inside the core material than in air, so flux crowds into the rod and \(B\) on the axis rises about 8×. But every loop still leaves the rod and returns through air, and that air section of the loop limits how much flux the same current can drive.

Same turns, current and measurement point. Now each flux loop closes entirely inside the core: \(B\) on the axis rises to 360 mT, about 100× the rod, while the field outside stays small. A second winding placed anywhere on the centre limb links nearly the same \(\Phi\), which is what makes a transformer possible.

Flux Linked by a Winding

A turn links flux when that flux passes through the surface bounded by the turn. In this sketch, the surface includes the core cross-section \(A_c\).

A winding links the flux once per turn. If each turn links the same flux:

\(\displaystyle \lambda=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\Phi_k=N\Phi\)

Faraday’s Law: Voltage Sets the Flux Change

Faraday’s law (terminal voltage, passive sign convention):

\(\displaystyle v_1=\frac{d\lambda_1}{dt}=N_1\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\)

\(\displaystyle \lambda_1(t)=\lambda_1(0)+\int_0^t v_1(\tau)\,d\tau\)

\(+20\ \mathrm V\) for \(5\ \mu\mathrm s\) gives \(\Delta\lambda_1=100\ \mu\mathrm{V\,s}\).

With \(N_1=50\) turns, \(\displaystyle \Delta\Phi=\frac{\Delta\lambda_1}{N_1}=2\ \mu\mathrm{Wb}\).

Shared Flux Explains the Voltage Ratio

If both windings link the same changing core flux:

\(\displaystyle v_1=N_1\frac{d\Phi}{dt},\qquad v_2=N_2\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\)

The voltage per turn is the same:

\(\displaystyle \frac{v_1}{N_1}=\frac{v_2}{N_2}\)

The dots specify matching voltage polarity. More turns give more induced voltage for the same flux change. Flux that is not shared is leakage, which we add to the model later.

Does an Unloaded Transformer Draw Current?

Leave the secondary terminals open: \(i_2=0\).

Apply an alternating voltage to the primary.

The ideal transformer alone predicts \(i_1=0\) because there is no load current.

A real winding still draws magnetizing current \(i_m\). The voltage sets how the flux changes, but flux in the core needs current in the winding to produce it (slide 7). That current is \(i_m\).

In a linear model the flux linkage is proportional to that current, \(\lambda_1=N_1\Phi=L_m i_m\). The constant \(L_m\) is the magnetizing inductance. Secondary open, losses neglected: \(i_1=i_m\).

Magnetizing Inductance: Large and Small

Linear magnetizing branch: \(\lambda_1=L_m i_m\), so

\(\displaystyle v_1=\frac{d\lambda_1}{dt}=L_m\frac{di_m}{dt}\)

Buck-inductor waveshapes: triangular \(\lambda_1\) and \(i_m\).

Under load, \(\displaystyle i_1=\frac{N_2}{N_1}i_2+i_m\).

Large \(L_m\) (mains transformer): \(i_m\approx0\), ideal element.

Small \(L_m\) (flyback, gapped core): delivered energy passes through \(i_m\), \(W=\lambda^2/2L_m\).

Transformer Volt-Second Balance and Core Size

As for the buck inductor, steady state requires volt-second balance: \(\int_0^{T_s}v_1\,dt=0\). Excess positive volt-seconds make \(i_m\) and flux drift upward each cycle, toward saturation.

Core size follows volt-seconds. From slide 9, \(\Delta\Phi=\int_0^{DT_s}v_1\,dt\,/N_1\approx V D/(N_1 f_s)\), and with \(\Delta\Phi=A_c\,\Delta B\): \(\Delta B\approx\frac{V D}{N_1}\cdot\frac{1}{A_c f_s}\).

\(V D/N_1\) is fixed by the conversion ratio. The limit is on the peak: \(B_\mathrm{max}<B_\mathrm{sat}\), with \(B_\mathrm{max}=\Delta B/2\) (bipolar swing), \(\Delta B\) (unipolar, from zero) or \(B_\mathrm{dc}+\Delta B/2\) (DC bias: flyback in CCM). Raise \(f_s\), shrink the core.

Leakage: Flux That Is Not Shared

Shared flux links both windings through the core.

Leakage flux links one winding without linking the other. Its return path passes through the surrounding air.

Equivalent Model with Leakage Inductance

\(L_m\) represents magnetization by the shared flux.

\(L_{l1}\) and \(L_{l2}\) represent leakage in series with each winding.

The primary terminal voltage includes the leakage drop:

\(\displaystyle v_1=v_m+L_{l1}\frac{di_1}{dt}\)

Reflecting Elements Through the Ideal Transformer

Let \(n=N_1/N_2\). The ideal element gives \(v_1=n\,v_2\) and \(i_1=i_2/n\), so

\(\displaystyle \frac{v_1}{i_1}=n^2\,\frac{v_2}{i_2}\)

Seen from the primary, an element on the secondary is the same element scaled by \(n^2\):

\(R\to n^2R,\qquad L\to n^2L,\qquad C\to C/n^2\)

Check it for \(L\) (same steps for \(R\), \(C\)): \(i_2=v_2/(j\omega L)\), \(i_1=i_2/n\), \(v_2=v_1/n\), so \(\displaystyle i_1=\frac{v_2}{n\,j\omega L}=\frac{v_1/n}{n\,j\omega L}=\frac{v_1}{j\omega\,(n^2L)}\)

Measuring the Model: Open and Short Circuit

The model of slide 15 with \(L_{l2}\) reflected to the primary.

Example: \(L_{\mathrm{oc}}=1.00\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(L_{\mathrm{sc}}=20\ \mu\mathrm{H}\) give \(L_{l1}\approx n^2L_{l2}\approx10\ \mu\mathrm{H}\) and \(L_m\approx990\ \mu\mathrm{H}\).

Secondary open, \(i_2=0\): no current enters the ideal primary.

\(L_{\mathrm{oc}}=L_{l1}+L_m\)

Secondary shorted, \(v_2=0\): the ideal primary is shorted too, so \(L_m\parallel n^2L_{l2}\).

\(L_{\mathrm{sc}}=L_{l1}+L_m\parallel n^2L_{l2}\approx L_{l1}+n^2L_{l2}\)

The \(\approx\) needs \(L_m\gg n^2L_{l2}\): true for grid transformers, phase-shifted full bridges, flybacks; not for resonant converters.

Splitting the leakage (2 measurements, 3 unknowns): assume \(L_{l1}\approx n^2L_{l2}\approx L_{\mathrm{sc}}/2\), so \(L_m\approx L_{\mathrm{oc}}-L_{\mathrm{sc}}/2\).

The Flyback Converter

  • A simple and very common isolated dc-dc converter
  • Typically for 1s to 10s of W
  • Some applications:
    • auxiliary supply for gate drivers or control boards
    • charging small batteries (phone, laptop, …)

Note the dots: with this secondary connection, turning \(Q_1\) on makes the diode reverse biased.

The Flyback Model We Analyse

The ideal transformer sets the winding ratio. The parallel \(L_m\) stores energy:

\(\displaystyle E_m=\tfrac12 L_m i_m^2\)

\(Q_{1}\) is on for \(DT_{s}\) and off for the rest of the period:

Flyback: Store Energy, Then Deliver It

Switch on: store energy

\(v_g\) sits across \(L_m\): \(i_m\) ramps up and the stored energy \(L_m i_m^2/2\) grows. The reversed secondary holds \(D_1\) off, so nothing leaves the transformer yet.

Switch off: deliver energy

\(i_m\) cannot stop: it transfers to the secondary through the turns ratio and \(D_1\) conducts. \(i_m\) ramps down as \(L_m\) delivers its stored energy to the output.

Two Operating States

\(v_{L}=v_{g}\)
\(i_{C}=-\frac{v}{R}\)
SRA: \(\;v_{L}=V_{g},\qquad i_{C}=-\frac{V}{R}\)

\(v_{L}=-\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\,v\)
\(i_{C}=\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\,i_{m}-\frac{v}{R}\)
SRA: \(\;v_{L}=-\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}V,\qquad i_{C}=\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}I_{m}-\frac{V}{R}\)

Steady State: The Averages First

With the two states in hand, we first solve for the steady-state averages:

  • the average capacitor voltage \(V\), and with it the conversion ratio \(M(D)=V/V_g\), from inductor volt-second balance on \(L_m\)
  • the average magnetizing current \(I_m\) from capacitor charge balance on \(C\)

The same two tools as for the buck and boost; only the state equations differ.

Inductor Volt-Second Balance: Solving for V

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=-\dfrac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}V\)

Apply volt-second balance to \(L_{m}\):

\(\displaystyle \langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\int_{0}^{T_{s}} v_{L}\,dt = 0\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[V_{g}DT_{s} - \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}V\,D'T_{s}\right] = V_{g}D - \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}V D'\)

Solving for \(V\), with \(D' = 1-D\):

\(\displaystyle V = \frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}} \cdot \frac{D}{1-D} \cdot V_{g}\)

The Conversion Ratio M(D)

\[M(D)=\frac{V}{V_{g}}=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}\cdot\frac{D}{1-D}\]

  • \(M = N_{2}/N_{1}\) at \(D = 0.5\); below that it steps down, above it steps up
  • \(D/(1-D)\) is the buck’s \(D\) times the boost’s \(1/(1-D)\): the flyback is a buck-boost with a transformer in it
  • The turns ratio is a free design choice: it sets where \(D\) sits for a given \(V/V_{g}\)

Charge Balance: Average Magnetizing Current

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=-V/R\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}I_{m}-V/R\)

Apply capacitor charge balance:

\(\displaystyle \langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\int_{0}^{T_{s}} i_{C}\,dt = 0\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[-\frac{V}{R}DT_{s} + \left(\frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}I_{m}-\frac{V}{R}\right)D'T_{s}\right]\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = -\frac{V}{R} + \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}I_{m}D'\)

\(\displaystyle \Rightarrow\; I_{m} = \frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}} \cdot \frac{1}{1-D} \cdot \frac{V}{R}\)

Next: The Ripple

The averages fix \(V\) and \(I_m\). Next, the waveshapes around them:

  • the magnetizing current ripple \(\Delta i_m\), from the slope \(v_L/L_m\) over the on interval
  • the output voltage ripple \(\Delta v\), from the slope \(i_C/C\) over the on interval

As for the buck: integrate the state equation over one interval.

Magnetizing Current Ripple

We know: \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}\) for \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\)

The inductor equation gives the slope of \(i_{m}\):

\(\displaystyle L_{m}\frac{di_{m}}{dt} = v_{L}\)

Over the on interval \(i_{m}\) rises by \(\Delta i_{m}\) (peak-to-peak):

\(\displaystyle \Delta i_{m} = \frac{1}{L_{m}}\int_{0}^{DT_{s}} v_{L}\,dt\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\Delta i_{m}} = \frac{V_{g}\,D\,T_{s}}{L_{m}}\)

Output Voltage Ripple

We know: \(\;i_{C}=-V/R\) for \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\)

The capacitor equation gives the slope of \(v\):

\(\displaystyle C\frac{dv}{dt} = i_{C}\)

Integrate over the on interval, where \(v\) falls by \(\Delta v\):

\(\displaystyle \Delta v = -\frac{1}{C}\int_{0}^{DT_{s}} i_{C}\,dt\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\Delta v} = \frac{V\,D\,T_{s}}{R\,C}\)

Finally: Switch Stress and DCM

Two more results close the flyback:

  • the maximum voltage across \(Q_1\): what the switch must block, and how the turns ratio sets it
  • the flyback in DCM: at light load \(i_m\) reaches zero and a third state appears, with \(D_1\) off as well. The background you need to work the DCM case yourself.

Maximum Voltage Across the Switch

While \(Q_{1}\) is off, \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\), \(D_{1}\) conducts and the output is reflected onto the primary:

\(\displaystyle v_{Q1} = v_{g} + \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\,v\)

Both terms are largest at the end of the off interval, where \(v\) has climbed to its peak:

\(\displaystyle V_{Q1,\max} = V_{g} + \frac{N_{1}}{N_{2}}\left(V + \frac{\Delta v}{2}\right)\)

A large \(N_{1}/N_{2}\) lowers \(I_{m}\) but raises the switch stress: the turns ratio trades one for the other.

The Flyback in DCM

Three states: ① \(Q_{1}\) on, ② \(D_{1}\) on for \(D_{2}T_{s}\), ③ both off, where \(v_{L}=0\) and \(i_{C}=-V/R\): \(C\) alone feeds the load.

\(D_{2}\) is set by the load, not the controller: find it with volt-second and charge balance.

\(i_{m}\) hits zero before \(T_{s}\) and \(D_{1}\) turns off, either:

  • at light load, in a flyback designed for CCM, or
  • at every load, when DCM is the design choice: a smaller \(L_{m}\), and \(D_{1}\) is already off when \(Q_{1}\) turns on
